title_tpl: Privilege Escalation via ioctl from {src} to {dst}
description_tpl: A malicious or compromised {src} process may send crafted ioctl commands to {dst} to gain elevated kernel privileges. Insufficient validation of caller credentials allows unprivileged callers to trigger privileged operations.
mitigations_tpl: Validate caller UID/GID and capabilities before executing privileged ioctl handlers in {dst}. Use kernel access-control checks (e.g. capable(), ns_capable()) and restrict the device node permissions.
attack_path_tpl: Attacker runs code as {src} → opens the {dst} device node → issues a privileged ioctl command without the required credential check → executes a privileged operation in {dst}

title_tpl: Insufficient Input Validation on ioctl Arguments to {dst}
description_tpl: ioctl arguments supplied by {src} are copied from user space into {dst} kernel handlers. Lack of size checks or type validation on the argument structure can lead to buffer overflows, integer overflows, or kernel memory corruption.
mitigations_tpl: Use copy_from_user() / copy_to_user() with explicit size bounds in {dst}. Validate all ioctl argument fields before use and reject unexpected values with -EINVAL.
attack_path_tpl: Attacker runs code as {src} → issues an ioctl to {dst} with out-of-range sizes, offsets or handles → {dst} acts on the unvalidated argument → kernel memory is corrupted

title_tpl: Denial of Service via Malformed ioctl to {dst}
description_tpl: A buggy or hostile {src} can send malformed or rapidly repeated ioctl commands to {dst}, potentially causing kernel panics, resource exhaustion, or deadlocks in the driver.
mitigations_tpl: Add rate-limiting and request queuing in {dst}. Ensure all error paths release locks and resources. Use kernel sanitizers (KASAN, lockdep) during development.
attack_path_tpl: Attacker runs code as {src} → repeatedly issues malformed or oversized ioctls to {dst} → {dst} exhausts memory, locks or worker threads → service is unavailable to legitimate callers

title_tpl: TOCTOU Race Condition on Shared Memory between {src} and {dst}
description_tpl: When {src} writes data to shared memory consumed by {dst}, a time-of-check/time-of-use window exists. An attacker controlling {src} can modify the shared buffer after {dst} has validated it but before it is used.
mitigations_tpl: Copy shared memory contents to a private kernel/process buffer before validation. Use atomic operations or memory barriers. Consider a single-copy protocol where {dst} owns the memory.
attack_path_tpl: Attacker maps the shared region used by {src} and {dst} → waits for {dst} to validate a field → rewrites that field before {dst} uses it → {dst} acts on data it believes it checked

title_tpl: Sensitive Data Leakage via Shared Memory from {src} to {dst}
description_tpl: Shared memory regions accessible to both {src} and {dst} may expose sensitive data (keys, tokens, intermediate state) to any process that can map the same region. Insufficient access controls or over-broad mapping permissions enable unintended disclosure.
mitigations_tpl: Restrict shared memory permissions to the minimum required. Avoid placing sensitive data in shared regions; prefer message-passing for secrets. Clear shared buffers after use.
attack_path_tpl: Attacker maps the shared region between {src} and {dst} → reads memory the producer left populated beyond the agreed fields → recovers data the consumer was never meant to see

description_tpl: The library loaded by {src} is resolved at runtime from the file system. An attacker with write access to the library search path can substitute a malicious library, causing {src} to execute attacker-controlled code under {src}'s privileges.
mitigations_tpl: Load {dst} from an OS-controlled, integrity-protected path. Verify the library signature or hash before loading. Set LD_LIBRARY_PATH carefully and avoid world-writable directories in the search path.
attack_path_tpl: Attacker plants a library named like {dst} earlier in the search path → {src} resolves and loads the attacker's copy → attacker code runs with {src}'s privileges

title_tpl: Insufficient Validation of Return Values from {dst}
description_tpl: Values returned by {dst} (especially buffers and sizes) may be invalid or attacker-controlled if the library was obtained from an untrusted source or has been compromised. {src} using these values without validation can lead to memory corruption or incorrect behaviour.
mitigations_tpl: Validate the size, type, and range of all values returned by {dst} before use in {src}. Treat the library boundary as an untrusted interface when the library is loaded from outside a controlled path.
attack_path_tpl: Attacker influences {dst} to return an error or short result → {src} proceeds without checking it → {src} continues on an uninitialised or attacker-chosen value

title_tpl: Symlink Attack on File Access from {src} to {dst}
description_tpl: If the file path resolved by {src} during open() can be replaced with a symbolic link by an attacker, {src} may operate on a different file than intended — potentially a privileged system file. This is a classic TOCTOU vulnerability.
mitigations_tpl: Use O_NOFOLLOW when opening files in world-writable directories. Prefer opening by file descriptor rather than path after initial resolution. Validate that the opened file's inode matches the expected target.
attack_path_tpl: Attacker replaces the path {src} opens with a symlink → {src} opens it without O_NOFOLLOW → the operation lands on a file the attacker chose

description_tpl: If the permissions on the file accessed by {src} are too broad, other processes can read or modify the file contents. Sensitive data written to the file by {src} could be exposed to lower-privileged processes.
mitigations_tpl: Apply the principle of least privilege to file permissions (e.g. 0600 for sensitive files). Use access control lists if finer grained control is needed. Avoid storing sensitive data in world-readable locations.
attack_path_tpl: Attacker runs code as {src} → opens a file whose permissions do not exclude it → reads contents outside {src}'s intended scope

title_tpl: Spoofing of {src} Identity Across Trust Boundary
description_tpl: Because this connection crosses a trust boundary, {dst} cannot reliably verify that the caller is genuinely {src}. A compromised or malicious process could impersonate {src} to gain access to {dst}'s services.
mitigations_tpl: Authenticate callers at the boundary using OS-level mechanisms (credentials, capabilities, selinux labels). Do not rely solely on the claimed identity of the caller.
attack_path_tpl: Attacker on the untrusted side of the boundary → presents the identity of {src} to {dst} → {dst} accepts it without authenticating the peer → attacker acts with {src}'s rights

title_tpl: Insufficient Audit Logging for {src}→{dst} Across Trust Boundary
description_tpl: Interactions crossing a trust boundary should be logged for auditability. Without logging, a malicious actor can make calls from {src} to {dst} that leave no trace, making forensic investigation difficult.
mitigations_tpl: Log all cross-boundary calls with caller identity, timestamp, and operation type. Ensure logs are written to a tamper-evident store that {src} cannot modify.
attack_path_tpl: Attacker acts across the boundary as {src} → performs a security-relevant operation on {dst} → no record identifies the caller → the action cannot be attributed afterwards

title_tpl: Data Leakage Across Trust Boundary from {dst} to {src}
description_tpl: Responses or error messages returned by {dst} to {src} across the trust boundary may expose internal state, memory addresses, or sensitive configuration. This is particularly dangerous when {src} is a less-privileged component.
mitigations_tpl: Sanitise all data returned across the boundary. Return generic error codes rather than detailed internal errors to lower-trust callers. Review API responses for inadvertent information leakage.
attack_path_tpl: Attacker runs code as {src} → requests data from {dst} across the trust boundary → {dst} returns more than the caller's level allows → attacker obtains higher-classification data

title_tpl: Denial of Service Against {dst} from Untrusted {src}
description_tpl: A malicious {src} operating outside {dst}'s trust boundary can flood {dst} with requests or send inputs designed to cause resource exhaustion, causing legitimate callers to be denied service.
mitigations_tpl: Implement rate limiting and request quotas per caller at the boundary. Ensure {dst} can shed load gracefully without affecting higher-priority callers.
attack_path_tpl: Attacker on the untrusted side → floods {dst} with requests across the boundary → {dst} has no per-caller quota → {dst} stops serving trusted callers

description_tpl: If {dst} performs operations based solely on input from {src} without re-validating authorisation, a compromised {src} can induce {dst} to perform actions exceeding {src}'s privilege level.
mitigations_tpl: Re-authorise every privileged operation in {dst} using the caller's verified credentials, not the caller's self-reported identity. Never grant elevated access based on an unchecked caller claim.
attack_path_tpl: Attacker runs code as {src} → crosses into {dst} across the trust boundary → {dst} applies the caller's privilege instead of re-deriving it → attacker operates at {dst}'s level
